svg.aria-label: Diagram: why a secondary subnet range is not required for alias IP ranges and is described as merely an organizational tool, what alias IP itself provides including automatic route installation and anti-spoofing checks, why a secondary range is the place address-based firewall separation still works and the source-tag gap that undermines it, and the three costs of a secondary range: no address reservation, no DNS, and a quota that counts ranges rather than addresses
svg.title: Secondary ranges and alias IP: an optional address space whose real product is a policy boundary
svg.text: A secondary range is not required for alias IP. It is an address space you can firewall.
The docs call it merely an organizational tool. The organization it buys is a policy boundary.
What a secondary range is, and is not
Every IPv4 subnet has exactly ONE primary range. Secondary ranges are optional, up to 170.
Alias IP ranges can come from the primary range OR a secondary range of the SAME subnet.
Use of alias IP ranges does not require secondary subnet ranges. These secondary subnet
ranges merely provide an organizational tool. That is the documentation, verbatim.
What alias IP itself buys, which is more than addressing
Google Cloud automatically installs VPC routes for primary and alias ranges. No route per
alias, and alias ranges do not count against route quotas.
Anti-spoofing checks verify that VMs do not send traffic with arbitrary source addresses.
The alternative is the point: static routes for container networking would be LESS SECURE,
because they require anti-spoofing to be disabled — it is off when IP forwarding is on.
The real reason to use a secondary range
Separating the ranges separates infrastructure (VMs) from services (containers), so you can
firewall alias addresses separately from a VM primary address. Post #63 found that subnet
boundaries carry no policy; a secondary range is where address-based separation still works.
BUT: alias ranges are NOT included when you specify sources by tag or service account.
So write those rules with source IP RANGES. A source-tag rule silently misses alias traffic.
What a secondary range costs you
NO RESERVATION: you cannot reserve an internal IP from a secondary range. Reserve from the
PRIMARY range instead and use it as a /32 alias — which undoes the separation above.
NO DNS: Google Cloud does not associate alias addresses with the host name. Ever.
NO SIZE CREDIT: quota counts RANGES, not addresses. A /32 and a /23 each cost one.
150 alias ranges per interface. So many tiny /32s exhaust the quota a few /24s would not.
Auto mode subnets have a primary range but NO secondary range — another thing #62 costs you.
Secondary ranges also consume the network-wide subnet-range quota, alongside primary and IPv6.
All addresses in a secondary range are usable; a primary range always loses four. So the
secondary range is cheaper per address and dearer per decision. Size few, size them large.
